processing: Fully oxidised Ceylon black tea from the estate's own factory, sold in grades such as BOP and BOPF.
harvest_season: Plucked year-round, as across Sri Lanka. Uva teas are generally most prized from the dry season in the middle of the year.
appearance_dry: Dark brown-black broken leaf, as usual for BOP-type Ceylon grades.
appearance_liquor: Bright coppery red, as is typical of Uva teas.
taste_profile: Specific notes are few. As with other Uva high-grown teas, expect a brisk, bright cup with some mellow sweetness and a light, almost wintergreen lift in the best seasonal lots.

brewing.notes: Western style. Broken grades extract fast; start at three minutes and take it from there.

vintage_note: Sold through the Colombo auction by grade and invoice, then resold by estate name, without a vintage year. Drink it within a year or two. Buyers looking for the classic Uva character tend to ask for dry-season lots, as with other estates in the district.
description:
Aislaby is an estate near Bandarawela in Sri Lanka's Uva High Grown district, at about 1,218 m. Tea people in Colombo know the name mostly from auction news: it has set several all-time price records, including Rs. 3,000 per kg for a BOPF in August 2022.

It makes black tea in the usual Ceylon grades in its own factory. The estate holds ISO 22000 and Rainforest Alliance certification and is run by Malwatte Valley Plantations PLC.

Detailed tasting notes are hard to come by, so go by the district: Uva teas tend to be brisk and bright, with a little mellow sweetness. Brew broken grades short, and judge with and without milk.

Retailers occasionally sell it as a single-estate BOP. Check the grade and ask when it was made. A price record for one auction lot says little about an ordinary pack.
history:
The estate's story, as told in a Sunday Times feature, begins in 1920, when Norman Bostock bought and planted the land and named it after the Aislaby he had roots in, in North Yorkshire. His son Mark later chaired the John Keells Group. The factory followed in 1936.

Reports differ on size, with 325 hectares in one and 463 hectares of tea gardens in another.
